definition: In machine learning, feature hashing, also known as the hashing trick (by analogy to the kernel trick), is a fast and space-efficient way of vectorizing features, i.e.
details: turning arbitrary features into indices in a vector or matrix. It works by applying a hash function to the features and using their hash values as indices directly (after a modulo operation), rather than looking the indices up in an associative array. In addition to its use for encoding non-numeric values, feature hashing can also be used for dimensionality reduction. This trick is often attributed to Weinberger et al. (2009), but there exists a much earlier description of this method published by John Moody in 1989.

explainer.lead: Feature hashing turns arbitrary features into positions in a fixed-size vector or matrix, without maintaining a lookup table for every possible feature. It is a fast, space-efficient way to vectorize non-numeric values and can also reduce dimensionality.

tiers.eli5: Imagine a fixed row of numbered boxes and a rule that turns each feature's name into a box number. You can then place features into boxes without first making a directory of every name you might see. Sometimes two names point to the same box, but using fewer boxes saves space.
tiers.practitioner: Hash each feature, take the hash modulo the chosen vector size, and use the result as its index. This avoids maintaining an associative array and keeps the representation at a fixed dimension. The main pitfall is collisions: distinct features can map to the same index, with smaller vectors generally leaving less room to separate them.
tiers.paperLevel: For feature f and output dimension d, compute i = h(f) mod d and use i as the feature's component in a vector or matrix. The method is often attributed to Weinberger et al. (2009), although John Moody published a description in 1989. Its mapping is not guaranteed to be one-to-one because different features can collide at the same index.

explainer.example: Suppose the output has 5 positions and the feature "color=blue" hashes to 17. Since 17 mod 5 = 2, that feature is placed at index 2, with no dictionary entry needed to assign its position.

usedIn.name: Non-numeric feature encoding
usedIn.detail: Converts arbitrary feature names or values directly into numeric vector or matrix indices.

usedIn.name: Dimensionality reduction
usedIn.detail: Maps features into a chosen fixed-size representation rather than assigning every feature its own dimension.

explainer.intuition: Instead of deciding in advance which column belongs to every possible feature, let a hash function make that decision on demand. A fixed-size output bounds the space needed, at the cost of allowing different features to share an index.
howItWorks: Start with an arbitrary feature and choose the output dimension d.
Apply a hash function to the feature to obtain a hash value.
Take that value modulo d to produce an index within the output.
Use the index directly in the vector or matrix, without consulting an associative array.
explainer.whyItMatters: It makes feature vectorization fast and space-efficient while supporting arbitrary features and a fixed output size. The same approach can reduce dimensionality when giving every feature a separate dimension would require too much space.
misconceptions: Feature hashing does not guarantee a unique index for every feature; collisions can occur.
It is not limited to encoding non-numeric values, since it can also be used for dimensionality reduction.
The output size is chosen in advance rather than growing as new feature names appear.
